sentences.text: Aepyornis was an extinct genus of elephant birds that lived only on Madagascar.
It was a ratite that could not fly and lacked a keel on its breast bone, sharing this trait with other flightless birds like the ostrich and kiwi.
Both species possessed small heads with straight, thick conical beaks, though the beak was proportionally larger in A. hildebrandti.
The neck of Aepyornis was proportionally long, containing 16 to 17 cervical vertebrae.
The wings of Aepyornis were vestigial.
The pelvic bones of Aepyornis were heavily fused, making their individual boundaries difficult to discern.
The hindlimbs were proportionally long and robust, with a particularly short and thick femur.
The terminal toe bones of Aepyornis were broad and not hooked.
Aepyornis eggs are the largest known for any amniote, with volumes of 5.6 to 13 litres, representing about 160 times the volume of a chicken egg.
Archaeological evidence suggests Aepyornis eggs regularly provided meals for entire human families.
The genus Aepyornis was described by I. Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire in 1851, though it was named by Geoffroy in 1850.
DNA from Aepyornis eggs was successfully extracted and published in 2010.
Brain endocasts show that Aepyornis had greatly reduced optic lobes, consistent with a nocturnal lifestyle.
Larger olfactory bulbs in A. maximus suggest it occupied forested habitats, while A. hildebrandti likely occupied open habitats.
A 2022 isotope study suggested A. hildebrandti was a mixed feeder with a large grazing component, while A. maximus was probably a browser.
An intact embryonic skeleton of Aepyornis was found in an egg that was 80-90% of the way through incubation.
Possible remnants of medullary bone used for egg calcium have been found in the femurs of A. maximus.
The closest living relative of Aepyornis is the New Zealand kiwi.
DNA comparisons suggest elephant birds diverged from New Zealand kiwis over 50 million years ago.
Aepyornis lived from the Late Pleistocene to the Holocene, between 0.129 and 0 million years ago.
Later DNA studies suggest Vorombe titan is indistinguishable from A. maximus and likely represents large females of that species.
It is debated whether Aepyornis extinction was a secondary effect of diseases transferred from domesticated fowl.
